Learning Objectives
Review the natural history of bone development and the pathophysiology associated with loss
of bone mineral density and osteoporosis.
Explain the epidemiology of and risk factors for osteoporosis.
Diagnose osteoporosis in clinical practice and review the importance of a multidisciplinary
approach for the management of osteoporotic fractures.
Recognize pharmacotherapy options for the management of osteoporosis and explain how to
select the most appropriate option.
Identify impending pathologic fractures, including those associated with chronic
diphosphonate use and metastatic disease, and the timing and method for prophylactic
stabilization.


Overview
Bone mass is acquired between ages 2 to 30 years, with peak bone mass (PBM)
occurring in individuals in their twenties. Failure to attain sufficient PBM during this
period is one of the main causes of osteoporosis, a condition characterized by low bone
mass and deterioration of normal bone architecture. This imbalance between bone
resorption and bone growth occurs slowly after attainment of PBM and escalates in
women after the onset of menopause. As bone architecture deteriorates, fracture risk
increases. This risk is aggravated by decreased mobility and other factors associated
with aging, including an increased risk of falls.
The World Health Organization defines osteoporosis (and osteopenia) according to a
patient’s T-score on bone mineral density (BMD) testing:
Normal BMD: within 1 standard deviation below PBM (T-score, 0 to -1.0)
Osteopenia: 1.0 to 2.5 standard deviations below PBM (T-score, -1.0 to -2.5)
Osteoporosis: more than 2.5 standard deviations below PBM (T-score, less than -2.5)
The T-score reflects a comparison with individuals at PBM, whereas the Z-score, another
bone density measurement, reflects a comparison with individuals of similar age.
In the absence of a BMD evaluation, clinical osteoporosis is defined based on a ground-
level fall resulting in a fracture.

Epidemiology
Osteoporosis is common, and the incidence of osteoporosis is increasing because of the
following factors:
Aging patient population
Association with chronic inflammatory diseases, such as diabetes mellitus and chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease, poor nutrition, and thyroid disorders
Increased use of medications that affect bone homeostasis
Proton pump inhibitors
Anticonvulsant medications
Antidepressants
Corticosteroids

Epidemiology
The incidence of osteoporosis continues to increase because of a rapidly aging patient
population and increased use of commonly prescribed medications that have a
deleterious effect on bone metabolism.1,2 Rates of osteoporosis are higher in patients
with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus, individuals with poor nutrition (including those
with morbid obesity), and patients with thyroid disorders. Costs associated with
osteoporosis management increased an estimated 118% over a recent 15-year period,
and the trend is expected to continue.3 Identification and management of osteoporosis
after a fracture is critical reduce the incidence of future fractures.
Etiology
Causes of decreased BMD are multifactorial and include genetic and environmental factors.
Many risk factors for osteoporosis are readily identified via a simple patient history.
In females, withdrawal of estrogen is one of the main causes of osteoporosis; estrogen
deficiency increases receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand (RANKL) expression.
Specific genes are associated with osteoporosis.


Etiology
Although osteoporosis traditionally is associated with postmenopausal women, poor
BMD also occurs in select younger patients with multiple risk factors and aging males. At
age 65 years, approximately 5% of males have osteoporosis compared with 24% of
females. Common risk factors include smoking, chronic alcohol use, use of medications
that alter BMD, and genetic predisposition. Modifiable risk factors, such as smoking and
medication use, cause osteoporosis via multiple mechanisms, including interruptions in
calcium homeostasis and intestinal absorption, dysregulation of sex hormone and
adrenocortical hormone metabolism, and increased activation of RANKL. Defects in
genes, such as COL1A1; vitamin D receptors; and LRP5, which codes for low-density
lipoprotein receptor-related protein, also are associated with osteoporosis.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Documenting fall risk and fracture history is important.
A thorough review of a patient’s medication list, past and present, is key.
Identifying the most common risk factors is simple.
Smoking
Alcohol abuse
Low body weight
Family history of hip fracture
Earlier age at onset of menopause
Fair complexion
The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) is a helpful validated model for calculating 10-year
fracture risk.4
Patients screened and found to be at risk for osteoporosis, including postmenopausal women
older than 65 years and individuals older than 50 years with risk factors, should undergo
additional studies to determine BMD.


Patient History
During an evaluation for osteoporosis, patients should be screened for fall risk and
educated about fall prevention regardless whether a fracture has been diagnosed.1
Physical therapy also may help prevent falls in patients at increased risk. Patients also
should be thoroughly screened for use of medications that decrease BMD, with
consideration given to discontinuing or changing medications that may predispose at-
risk patients to fracture. Commonly prescribed medications associated with decreased
BMD include anticonvulsants, antidepressants, glucocorticoids, and proton pump
inhibitors. A multidisciplinary approach is most effective.
The FRAX, a model for predicting a patient’s 10-year risk for fracture, may help guide
medical decision making during the work up and management of metabolic bone
disease.5 Dissimilar from current guidelines on the diagnosis and management of
osteoporosis, which focus on postmenopausal women, the FRAX is an effective tool for
evaluating men and younger patients with risk factors who may otherwise be missed. In
addition, the FRAX calculates the 10-year fracture risk without BMD values from a dual-
energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan, making it a good adjunctive screening tool for
osteoporosis.
The National Osteoporosis Foundation recommends BMD testing for all postmenopausal
women older than 65 years, postmenopausal women older than 50 years with risk
factors, and individuals older than 50 years with a history of fracture. Testing also is
recommended in all men older than 70 years and men older than 50 years with risk
factors6 (Resource 1).
Physical Examination
Patients with osteoporosis commonly present after a fracture from minor trauma (ie, ground-
level fall).
In patients with a hip fracture, examination of the spine and wrist also is important;
tenderness in either area often indicates additional injuries.


Physical Examination
Osteoporosis often is diagnosed only after a fracture has occurred; this is especially true
in men. In patients with a fracture after minor trauma osteoporosis should be suspected,
with screening, patient education, and the initiation of pharmacologic therapy indicated.
Missed injuries are possible in patients with a hip fracture, and the entire skeleton
should be thoroughly examined to identify less obvious injuries, including vertebral
compression and distal radius fractures. Although osteoporosis classically is associated
with fractures of the hip, wrist, shoulder, and spine, any low-energy geriatric fracture
should prompt additional workup for and management of osteoporosis.
Imaging Studies
Plain Radiography
Radiographic appearance
Osteopenia (Figure 1)
Thinning of the cortices
Loss of trabeculae

Figure 1 AP radiograph of the pelvis of an elderly female patient with low back pain
demonstrates diffuse osteopenia of the pelvic bones but no fracture. The patient’s symptoms
persisted; therefore, MRI was performed and revealed an insufficiency fracture of the sacral ala.
(Courtesy of Jim Fiechtl, MD, Franklin, TN.)

Plain Radiography
Technically, plain radiographs can detect osteopenia but cannot define osteoporosis.
Plain radiographs obtained after trauma or for other reasons may be assessed for
features of osteopenia, such as a bony trabecular pattern and thickness of the
diaphyseal cortex. A chest radiograph may reveal prior osteoporotic injuries, including
healed rib fractures or chronic compression fractures of the thoracic spine. Because
many patients treated for an osteoporotic hip fracture never begin pharmacotherapy to
reduce their risk for subsequent fracture, cephalomedullary devices or hemiarthroplasty
stems observed incidentally on other radiographs, including those obtained during
orthopaedic workup for knee osteoarthritis or other diagnoses, may indicate the need
for additional workup and possible management of osteoporosis.

Advanced Imaging Studies (CT, MRI, Bone Scintigraphy)
Limited role in the diagnosis of osteoporosis.
MRI may aid in the diagnosis of occult stress fractures of the femur in patients with chronic
diphosphonate use.
Although CT is not indicated to document bone density, a CT scan obtained for other reasons
may be useful for calculating bone density based on Hounsfield units or identifying sarcopenia
(an independent predictor of mortality after hip fracture).7,8

Advanced Imaging Studies (CT, MRI, Bone Scintigraphy)
Similar to radiography, CT has a limited role in the diagnosis of osteoporosis but may
provide valuable information about existing disease if obtained for other reasons. For
example, CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis may reveal prior compression fractures of
the spine, fractures of the superior or inferior pubic ramus and/or sacrum, or evidence
of a prior hip fracture. In patients who have not already been diagnosed with
osteoporosis, workup and management of osteoporosis should be considered. CT scans
that include the lumbar vertebrae or hip have been used to correlate Hounsfield units
with BMD and may substitute for a DEXA scan. In addition, axial CT scans of the pelvis
may reveal sarcopenia (ie, loss of muscle mass that is an important predictor of mortality
after hip fracture).
MRI has an extremely limited role in the management of osteoporosis. However, in
patients with long-term diphosphonate use and in whom a stress fracture of the
subtrochanteric femur is suspected despite normal radiographs, MRI may indicate that
prophylactic fixation is warranted.
Bone Density Testing
Preferred imaging modality to document bone density and the presence or absence of
osteopenia/osteoporosis
DEXA


Bone Density Testing
Although plain radiographs and advanced imaging studies may suggest underlying bone
metabolic disease, they are not a substitute for formal bone density testing. Instead,
DEXA remains the preferred imaging modality for quantifying BMD and diagnosing
osteoporosis. DEXA is routinely performed in three locations: the hip, spine, and distal
radius. Bone density may differ among the three areas, and values in the hip and spine
are most often used for determining the need for management, the risk for subsequent
hip fracture, and the response to pharmacologic management (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Dual x-ray absorptiometry scans of the hip (A) and the lumbar spine (B) of a 53-
year-old man with Fabry disease show assessment of bone mineral density. T scores of
−4.2 and −4.3, respectively, were determined. (Courtesy of Dr. Caroline Lebreton and
Raymond Poincaré Chu, Garches, France.)
Management
Nonsurgical/Pharmacologic Management

Indications
Documented osteoporosis (T-score
Osteopenia (T-score
History of low-energy fracture
Pharmacology
Supplemental calcium (1200 mg/d) and vitamin D intake (800 IU/d)
Antiresorptive therapy
Diphosphonates (first-line pharmacotherapy)
Selective estrogen receptor modulators
Calcitonin (nasal spray)
Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor)
Anabolic therapy
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)/analogues: teriparatide, abaloparatide
Sclerostin antibody: romosozumab

Nonsurgical/Pharmacologic Management
All patients at risk for metabolic bone disease should treated with calcium (1200 mg/d)
and vitamin D (800 IU/d) at doses sufficient to support bone homeostasis and prevent
additional decline. A meta-analysis of multiple clinical trials demonstrated that
supplementation with calcium and vitamin D improves BMD and reduces the incidence
of fracture in postmenopausal women;9-11 however, calcium and vitamin D
supplementation alone rarely is sufficient to manage osteoporosis because adherence to
management has been low historically. Therefore, diphosphonates are the most
commonly prescribed first-line pharmacotherapy. A wide body of literature supports
diphosphonate use, which is well tolerated in most patients.12 In patients who cannot
tolerate diphosphonates or in patients in whom diphosphonates are contraindicated, a
different antiresorptive therapy may be used or anabolic therapy should be considered.
Although antiresorptive medications prevent bone breakdown by inhibiting osteoclast
activity, anabolic agents have the added benefit of increasing BMD over time. Sustained

use of teriparatide, abaloparatide, and romosozumab is associated with not only
increases in BMD but also decreased risk of fracture.
Mechanism of Action/Adverse Effects
The potency of diphosphonates (pyrophosphate analogues) is related to their chemical
structure.
Nitrogen-containing versus non?nitrogen-containing drugs
Mechanism: leads to osteoclast apoptosis
Inhibits protein prenylation
Acts via the mevalonate pathway
Specifically inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate
Disrupts the ruffled border of osteoclasts
Adverse effects
Myalgias, bone pain, or weakness (in as many as one-third of patients)
Gastric irritation (if delivered orally)
Osteonecrosis of the jaw
Patients who are candidates for diphosphonate therapy should undergo a dental
evaluation before beginning treatment.
Atypical femur fractures
Occur with chronic use; drug holidays should be considered after long-term use.
Denosumab
Human monoclonal antibody targeting RANKL
Acts as a decoy receptor, blocking interactions between RANKL and receptor activator of
nuclear factor-kappa B
Infections have been reported with use
Anabolic therapies
Intermittent PTH (teriparatide)
Mechanism: N-terminus 1-34 amino acid sequence of PTH; the precise mechanism is
unknown; however, PTH most likely has direct and indirect positive effects on osteoblast
differentiation, function, and survival.
Adverse effects: mild hypercalcemia
Contraindications: hypercalcemia, history of primary bone malignancy, Paget disease, age
younger than 25 years

Sclerostin monoclonal antibody (romosozumab)
Mechanism: inhibits sclerostin, which acts in the WNT signaling pathway of bone
metabolism, making it uniquely anabolic and antiresorptive
Adverse effects
Headache, arthralgias, and injection site pain are common.
Cardiovascular events
Atypical femur fracture

Mechanism of Action/Adverse Effects
Diphosphonates are non?nitrogen containing or nitrogen containing, with all commonly
prescribed modern medications falling into the latter category. The drugs may be
administered orally or intravenously; however, intravenous administration (ie, often just
once per year) ensures greater adherence than daily oral administration. These
medications classically have been associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw (very rare); in
addition, the prevalence of atypical femur fractures recently has increased with long-
term use in many patients (ie, incidence directly related to duration of use). In 2016, the
American Society for Bone and Mineral Research published guidelines related to
diphosphonates and the risk of atypical femur fractures, recommending a drug holiday
after 3 to 5 years of use; however, the society added that discontinuation of
management should be determined on a case-by-case basis, considering a patient’s
overall fracture risk.13
In recent years, denosumab has emerged as an effective alternative to diphosphonates.
By acting as a decoy receptor for RANKL, denosumab inhibits osteoclast differentiation
and activation; however, denosumab is not selective to bone, and systemic
complications, especially serious infections, have been reported with its use.14 In
addition, denosumab should not be used in patients who are taking chronic
immunosuppressive medications or patients who are immunosuppressed for other
reasons.
Diphosphonates remain the first-line treatment option for the management of metabolic
bone disease; however, they should not be used in patients with an atypical femur

12/18

fracture; should not be used for long terms, requiring discontinuation, and should not be
used in patients with a refracture despite therapy. Dissimilar from diphosphonates,
anabolic drugs increase BMD. Teriparatide and abaloparatide increase BMD in the spine
and hip; however, because of the theoretic risk for osteosarcoma, both drugs should be
discontinued after 24 months and are contraindicated in patients younger than 25 years.
Paget disease and hypercalcemia are additional contraindications to PTH analogues.
Romosozumab is a recently approved medication that is uniquely designed to activate
anabolic and antiresorptive pathways. Romosozumab inhibits sclerostin, a protein
involved in regulating the WNT pathway of bone metabolism. Despite its obvious
benefits, in large-scale clinical trials, romosozumab has been associated with major
cardiac adverse effects, limiting its use to patients with refractory osteoporosis who are
unable to be treated with antiresorptive agents and/or PTH analogues15,16 (Resource 2).
Surgical Management
Indications
Decreased BMD alone does not warrant surgical management.
Surgical management is intended to treat and prevent impending fractures resulting from
osteoporosis and other pathologic disease processes affecting the skeleton.
Atypical femur fractures
Benign bone tumors
Malignancies affecting the skeleton
Metastatic disease
Lymphoma and myeloma
Osteopetrosis
Paget disease of bone

Indications
Osteoporotic fractures commonly require surgical management, especially if they
involve the hip. Although osteoporotic fractures rarely require additional prophylactic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:30 PM
AAOS | Osteoporosis and Pathologic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002097
13/18

management, protecting as much of the bone as possible during surgical management is
beneficial. For example, cephalomedullary screws should be placed in fractures of the
femoral shaft to prevent future fracture of the femoral neck. Atypical femur fractures
resulting from lateral cortical thickening often are a technical challenge during surgical
management; nails remain the standard of care for these simple fracture patterns, and
prolonged time to union is expected.17
Careful consideration of the contralateral femur also is paramount; thigh pain is a
harbinger of impending fracture even if radiographs appear normal, and advanced
imaging via MRI may be necessary to identify an occult fracture. If thigh pain is present,
nonsurgical management is associated with a high rate of subsequent fracture;
therefore, prophylactic nailing should be strongly considered in these patients.18 In
patients with an atypical fracture, diphosphonates must be discontinued, with initiation
of another medication, usually an anabolic medication, such as teriparatide, to manage
osteoporosis (Resource 3).
If metastatic disease affects the skeleton, management of associated fractures and
prophylaxis of impending fractures require careful consideration. The location and type
of bony lesions and the presence of pain may affect surgical decision making. In patients
without known metastatic disease, a secondary malignancy or primary bone tumor
should be considered. Lesions that are painful, lytic, and in the proximal femur
represent a classic triad requiring urgent prophylactic fixation. Scoring systems, such as
the Mirels criteria, may help predict the patients most likely to benefit from prophylactic
fixation before pathologic fracture. During preoperative planning, imaging studies of the
entire involved bone must be obtained. Intraoperatively, as much of the affected bone as
possible should be protected; longer nails, longer plates, or a combination of implants
may be necessary to span multiple involved areas of the bone. Postoperatively,
additional workup of the entire skeleton is essential to ensure that no lesions warranting
prophylactic measures were missed. A multidisciplinary approach alongside internists
and oncologists also will help prevent future fractures.
The type of malignant bone lesion should be identified preoperatively because some
bone tumors are notoriously vascular and may lead to rapid intraoperative hemorrhage.
Thyroid cancer and renal cell carcinoma classically are associated with hemorrhage.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:30 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002097
14/18

Patients with renal cell carcinoma, in particular, should undergo vascular embolization,
generally within 72 hours of the initiation of surgical treatment. Multiple myeloma also
may be associated with bleeding, especially if reaming is performed.
Two additional conditions that predispose patients to pathologic fractures are
osteopetrosis and Paget disease. Although rare, osteopetrosis (or marble bone disease)
is the result of a genetic defect affecting osteoclast differentiation and development.
Radiographs demonstrate obliteration of the medullary canal, and fractures are
common. Preexisting long bone deformities and lack of an endosteum make surgical
fixation and prophylaxis difficult. Plates are necessary and may require contouring,
whereas the very dense bone also may require special drills and saws. Dissimilar from
osteopetrosis, Paget disease occurs later in life and involves dysregulation of osteoclast
function. Many affected patients are asymptomatic; however, deformity often is present,
and pain on presentation should alert the clinician to an impending fracture or
malignant degeneration (<1% of patients). Pharmacologic therapy includes
diphosphonates, with surgical management reserved for impending fractures, most
commonly of the femoral neck.
